Learning Rate Scaling across LoRA Ranks and Transfer to Full Finetuning
Nan Chen

Abstract
[id=abstract1.1] Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a standard tool for parameter-efficient finetuning of large models. While it induces a small memory footprint, its training dynamics can be surprisingly complex as they depend on several hyperparameters such as initialization, adapter rank, and learning rate. In particular, it is unclear how the optimal learning rate scales with adapter rank, which forces practitioners to re-tune the learning rate whenever the rank is changed. In this paper, we introduce Maximal-Update Adaptation (μ\muA), a theoretical framework that characterizes how the “optimal” learning rate should scale with model width and adapter rank to produce stable, non-vanishing feature updates under standard configurations. μ\muA is inspired from the Maximal-Update Parametrization (μ\muP) in pretraining.
Our analysis leverages techniques from hyperparameter transfer and reveals that the optimal learning rate exhibits different scaling patterns depending on initialization and LoRA scaling factor.
Specifically, we identify two regimes: one where the optimal learning rate remains roughly invariant across ranks, and another where it scales inversely with rank.
We further identify a configuration that allows learning rate transfer from LoRA to full finetuning, drastically reducing the cost of learning rate tuning for full finetuning.
Experiments across language, vision, vision–language, image generation, and reinforcement learning tasks validate our scaling rules and show that learning rates tuned on LoRA transfer reliably to full finetuning.

1 Introduction
Figure 1: LoRA finetuning with standard design choices.
[id=S1.p1.1] The widespread availability of large pretrained models has made finetuning the standard approach to adapt a general-purpose model to a specific downstream task (Radford et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019).
At the same time, model capability typically improves with scale, with state-of-the-art language and vision models now reaching hundreds of billions of parameters (Liu et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025).
The improvement in performance with scale makes larger models attractive to practitioners, but it also makes full finetuning (FFT) increasingly expensive. While FFT remains the standard for tasks such as instruction-tuning (Biderman et al., 2024), parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) has become a default approach in many settings (Han et al., 2024).
(a) Init[A], α=1\alpha=1
(b) Init[A], α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1}
(c) Init[B], α=1\alpha=1
Figure 2: Learning rate sweeps for three standard LoRA configurations on Llama-3.2-1B (Tulu3). Each panel plots final training loss (EMA-smoothed) versus log-scale learning rate log2⁡(η)\log_{2}(\eta) for multiple ranks (colored) and FFT (red). Large markers indicate the optimal learning rate for each rank; the dashed red line marks the optimal FFT learning rate. The y-axis is clipped for readability.
[id=S1.p2.1] Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) is arguably the most popular parameter-efficient finetuning method. It adds a low-rank factorization α​B​A\alpha BA to the (frozen) pretrained weight matrix W⋆∈ℝn×nW^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, where B∈ℝn×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, A∈ℝr×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}, rr is the LoRA rank, and α\alpha is a scaling multiplier. Only BB and AA are trainable in this setting.
[id=S1.p3.1] Deploying LoRA in practice requires several design choices beyond the rank rr.
To start from a no-op adapter, practitioners typically initialize one factor to random values and the other to zero; we denote these two common choices as Init[A] (random AA, B=0B=0) and Init[B] (random BB, A=0A=0) (Hayou et al., 2024b).
In addition, common implementations use different rank-dependent multipliers, typically α∈{1,r−1,r−1/2}\alpha\in\{1,\,r^{-1},\,r^{-1/2}\} (Kalajdzievski, 2023; Biderman et al., 2024); Figure 1 summarizes these standard choices.
Because LoRA update is bilinear in AA and BB, the initialization, multiplier α\alpha, rank rr, and learning rate η\eta are coupled and jointly determine the effective update magnitude. This coupling makes hyperparameter tuning brittle in practice.
Changing the rank or switching between initialization and multiplier choices can render a previously optimal learning rate suboptimal, forcing costly re-tuning.
Figure 2 provides a representative example on Llama-3.2-1B finetuned on the Tulu3 dataset, showing end-of-training loss as a function of learning rate for multiple ranks under three common configurations.
Under Init[A] with constant α=1\alpha=1, the best learning rate decreases with rank rr (Figure 2(a)).
Setting α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} while keeping Init[A] yields a different pattern: the optimal learning rate becomes approximately rank-invariant, but the stable range is narrow—small increases above the optimum cause divergence (Figure 2(b)).
With Init[B] and constant α=1\alpha=1, the optimal learning rate is again rank-invariant and now aligns with the FFT optimum (Figure 2(c)).
Notably, this optimal rate is more than an order of magnitude smaller than under Init[A] with α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1}.
Taken together, these experiments show that the learning rate–rank relationship changes qualitatively across initialization and multiplier choices.
This raises a natural question: how does the optimal learning rate η\eta depend on rank rr?
[id=S1.p4.1] To answer this question, we analyze LoRA finetuning in the joint limit n,r→∞n,r\to\infty.
Building on prior works analyzing infinite-width networks (Yang and Hu, 2020; Yang and Hu, 2021; Hayou et al., 2024b; Hayou et al., 2024a), we study how initialization, multiplier α\alpha, and learning rate η\eta jointly govern the magnitude of LoRA updates under a tractable theoretical setup.
This allows us to characterize when LoRA updates remain bounded yet non-vanishing in the large-nn, large-rr regime—avoiding instability while ensuring learning does not stall. We call this regime the Maximal-Update Adaptation (μ\muA).
From this analysis, we derive explicit scaling prescriptions for how the learning rate should depend on model width and LoRA rank under each configuration.
These prescriptions explain why some configurations (e.g., Init[A] with constant α\alpha) require the learning rate to decrease with rank, while others (e.g., Init[B] with constant α\alpha) admit rank-invariant learning rates.
Our analysis also connects LoRA to FFT.
For Init[B] with constant α\alpha, the learning rate scaling that ensures stable feature learning matches that of FFT under the same assumptions.
This matching is a necessary condition for hyperparameter transfer between the two regimes.
[id=S1.p5.1] We verify our theory through extensive experiments spanning diverse tasks, modalities, and training paradigms.
Across all settings, the observed learning rate–rank patterns consistently match our derived scaling rules, confirming that μ\muA scaling rules generalize across architectures and domains. Our contributions are summarized as follows:
[id=S1.I1.i1] •
[id=S1.I1.i1.p1.1] We introduce μ\muA (Maximal-Update Adaptation), a theoretical framework for LoRA finetuning dynamics in the joint limit n,r→∞n,r\to\infty and characterize how the optimal learning rate scales with model width and adapter rank to ensure maximal (stable) adaptation.
[id=S1.I1.i2] •
[id=S1.I1.i2.p1.1] Our analysis reveals two distinct regimes: one where the optimal learning rate scales inversely with rank, and one in which it remains rank-invariant. We identify a LoRA configuration where the optimal learning rate matches that of FFT (transfer from LoRA to FFT).
[id=S1.I1.i3] •
[id=S1.I1.i3.p1.1] Extensive experiments demonstrate that μ\muA scaling rules guarantee learning rate transfer across LoRA ranks and from LoRA and to FFT.
[id=S2]
2 Related Works
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Parameter-efficient finetuning.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] PEFT techniques fall into three main categories (Han et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2025): (i) selectively updating a subset of parameters (Collobert and Weston, 2008; Guo et al., 2021; Liao et al., 2023); (ii) adding lightweight adapters (Rebuffi et al., 2017; Houlsby et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2020; He et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022); or (iii) tuning continuous prompts (Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023).
LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) exemplifies the additive method and has inspired numerous variants targeting efficiency (Valipour et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Dettmers et al., 2023; Kopiczko et al., 2024; Ke et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024b; Hayou et al., 2025) and stability (Hayou et al., 2024a; Hayou et al., 2024b; Yen et al., 2025).
Recent studies compare LoRA and FFT across gradient alignment (Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), expressive power (Zeng and Lee, 2024), and spectral structure of weight updates (Shuttleworth et al., 2024).
Complementing these studies, we identify a LoRA configuration where the optimal learning rate matches that of FFT, guaranteeing learning rate transfer between the two methods.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
Design choices of LoRA.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] Standard schemes randomly initialize either AA or BB using established techniques (Glorot and Bengio, 2010; He et al., 2015), setting the other to zero.
Alternative methods initialize weights from pretrained weights (Büyükakyüz, 2024; Meng et al., 2024), deterministic orthogonal bases (Zhang et al., 2025), downstream data (Yang et al., 2024b; Paischer et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), or quantized models (Li et al., 2024b).
Prior theoretical analyses of initialization (Hayou et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025) focus on the infinite-width regime and treat the rank as constant; in contrast, we study the joint limit where both width nn and rank rr grow.
For the LoRA multiplier α\alpha, the original LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) uses α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} to keep update magnitudes controlled, rsLoRA (Kalajdzievski, 2023) proposes α=r−1/2\alpha=r^{-1/2} for stability at larger ranks, and recent works increasingly adopt α=1\alpha=1 (Gabrielsson et al., 2024; Biderman et al., 2024; Charakorn et al., 2025). Schulman (2025) empirically studies LoRA design choices but provides only heuristic rules for learning rate transfer between LoRA and FFT (e.g. dividing LoRA’s learning rate by 10 to obtain FFT’s learning rate). Another empirical work by Milsom et al. (2025) introduced a general rule for learning rate transfer across LoRA ranks but did not provide any explanation to the observed scaling rules. None of these works provide a theoretical analysis of learning rate transfer with LoRA finetuning. In this paper, we propose a principled approach to learning rate transfer across LoRA ranks and from LoRA to FFT.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
Asymptotic scaling analysis.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Our analysis builds on prior works analyzing the asymptotic behavior of neural networks as width approaches infinity (Yang and Hu, 2020; Yang and Hu, 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Hayou et al., 2024b; Hayou et al., 2024a).
Related works apply similar frameworks to analyze depth scaling (Hayou et al., 2019; Hayou et al., 2021; He et al., 2023; Hayou and Yang, 2023; Noci et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024a).
Most closely related to ours are Hayou et al. (2024b); Hayou et al. (2024a), which analyze LoRA finetuning in the limit n→∞n\to\infty but treat the rank rr as constant.
This analysis does not reveal how training dynamics depend on the rank rr.
Here, we analyze the joint limit n,r→∞n,r\to\infty, yielding scaling prescriptions that depend on both network width and LoRA rank.
Empirically, the optimal learning rate closely match derived scaling rules.

3.2 Stable Feature Learning
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] We aim to understand how feature updates behave as a function of model width nn and LoRA rank rr. For this purpose, we consider the setting where both nn and rr grow, subject to r≤nr\leq n.

[id=S3.Thmtheorem7.p1.1] We say LoRA induces stable feature learning if the dynamics are stable (Definition 3.5), and Δ​ZBt=Θ⁡(1)\Delta Z_{B}^{t}=\Theta(1) for all t≤Tt\leq T.

4 Maximal-Update Adaptation (μ\muA)
[id=S4.p1.1] We now state the learning rate scaling rules that guarantee stable feature learning under Init[A] and Init[B].
Full proofs and derivations (including the scaling of each δti\delta_{t}^{i}) appear in Appendix A.
Our analysis relies on two assumptions: (i) bounded forward and backward signals at each step, and (ii) a SignSGD update rule that uses the sign of the gradient, serving as a tractable proxy for the Adam optimizer.

[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We highlight the following key insights drawn from the corollary.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] Learning rate scaling with rank.
For a fixed model width nn, the relationship between the optimal learning rate and rank rr depends on the choice of α\alpha.
With α=1\alpha=1, the learning rate decreases as η∝r−1/2\eta\propto r^{-1/2}: increasing the rank by 4×4\times requires halving the learning rate, consistent with Figure 2(a).
In contrast, setting α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} absorbs the rank dependence, yielding a rank-invariant learning rate that depends only on width, consistent with Figure 2(b).
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1] Intermediate feature scaling.
The intermediate features ZAtZ_{A}^{t} grow with width nn but shrink with rank when α∈{1,r−1/2}\alpha\in\{1,r^{-1/2}\}.
For α=1\alpha=1, doubling the rank reduces the intermediate feature scale by 2\sqrt{2}, which can improve internal numerical stability in wide models where large intermediate activations have been identified as a source of training instability (Hayou et al., 2024b).

5 Experiments
[id=S5.p1.1] Our experiments verify μ\muA scaling rules empirically and learning rate transfer from LoRA to FFT.
We examine three regimes: supervised finetuning (SFT) across diverse architectures, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and text-to-image diffusion model finetuning.
[id=S5.SS1]
5.1 Experimental Setup
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1]
Unified finetuning recipe.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We use a unified finetuning recipe across all experiments.
Specifically, we use AdamW with weight decay of 0.010.01 and global-norm gradient clipping of 1.01.0.
The learning rate warms up linearly over the first 5%5\% of training steps to its peak (η\eta), then follows a cosine decay to 0.1×0.1\times the peak over the remaining steps.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2]
SFT setting.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We experiment with five public base models:
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1] Decoder-only language models.
For instruction tuning, we tune Llama-3.2-1B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) on the Tulu-3 supervised finetuning mixture (Lambert et al., 2024).
For long-context reasoning, we train Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025) on the OpenThoughts-114k (Guha et al., 2025).
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1] Encoder-only models.
We finetune RoBERTa-large (Liu et al., 2019) on the ANLI benchmark (Nie et al., 2020) and adapt ViT-Huge/14 (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) to ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009).
Following prior work (Guo et al., 2024), we fix the learning rate of the classification head at 10−310^{-3} and sweep only the LoRA learning rate.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p4.1] Vision–language model.
For multimodal instruction following, we finetune Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) on LLaVA-Instruct-Mix, containing image–instruction pairs.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3]
RLVR setting.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] We adapt Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) to GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021) with GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).
The reward is based on answer correctness and format compliance.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4]
Text-to-image diffusion model finetuning.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] We finetune Stable-Diffusion-v1.5 (Rombach et al., 2022) on the Naruto-BLIP-Captions (Cervenka, 2022) dataset.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5]
Evaluation protocol.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1] We compare three LoRA configurations: Init[A] with α=1\alpha=1, Init[A] with α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1}, and Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1.
For each configuration, we sweep learning rate η\eta (peak learning rate) on a log2\log_{2}-scale grid with multiplicative steps of 2×2\times and select the best value independently for (i) final training loss (EMA-smoothed) and (ii) a task-specific validation metric.
For RLVR, we select learning rates by final training reward; for diffusion models, by validation FID (Heusel et al., 2017).
More details are in Appendix B.

[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6]
Theory–experiment alignment.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1] Our scaling rules characterize the leading-order dependence of the stable learning rate on width nn and rank rr in the joint limit (n,r)→∞(n,r)\to\infty.
In practice, however, finetuning at finite width and rank introduces two deviations from the asymptotic prediction.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p2.1] Finite-size effects.
When (n,r)(n,r) are finite, constant factors and lower-order terms can shift the optimal learning rate. These shifts are more pronounced for smaller ranks, where the large-rr asymptotics are less accurate.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p3.1] Discrete learning rate grid.
We sweep learning rates on a log2\log_{2}-spaced grid.
The reported optimum is the best value among discrete points.
When the loss landscape is flat near the true optimum, adjacent grid points perform similarly, and training noise may determine which one appears best.
[id=S5.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p4.1] Accordingly, we evaluate the scaling rules by qualitative trends rather than exact numerical agreement.
For configurations predicted to be rank-invariant, we expect optimal learning rates to cluster within one grid step (2×2\times).
For rank-dependent configurations, we expect the optimum to change monotonically with rank and to span multiple grid points.

5.2 SFT Results
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1]
Init[A] with α=1\alpha=1 (Figures 3, 2(a))
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] For a fixed base model (i.e., fixed width nn), our theory in Table 1 predicts that the optimal learning rate scales as η∝r−1/2\eta\propto{r}^{-1/2} with rank.
This prediction is broadly supported by the experiments: as rank increases, the best-performing learning rate monotonically shifts toward smaller values.
Since each figure plots log2⁡(η)\log_{2}(\eta) on the X-axis, a 4×4\times increase in rank should shift the optimum leftward by one unit (i.e., a 2×2\times reduction in learning rate)—a pattern clearly visible across most models.
We observe minor deviations on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, where both r=16r=16 and r=64r=64 attain their minimum loss at the same learning rate.
We attribute this to the learning rate grid discretization: as shown in Figure 3(a), the loss curves for r=4r=4 and r=16r=16 flatten near the optimum.
Moreover, models finetuned with Init[A] and α=1\alpha=1 are sensitive to large learning rates: increasing the learning rate by 2×2\times beyond the optimum can substantially degrade training loss or cause divergence, particularly for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and RoBERTa-large.
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] While we report results for α=1\alpha=1 here, our theory holds for any rank-independent constant α\alpha. Since α=2\alpha=2 is a common default in practice, we verify in Appendix C.1 that the same scaling behavior persists for α∈{2,4}\alpha\in\{2,4\}.
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2]
Init[A] with α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} (Figures 4, 2(b))
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] According to our theory, for a fixed base model, the optimal learning rate should be independent of LoRA rank under this setting.
The experimental results support this prediction: for all models, the optimal learning rates across ranks fall within a narrow range (typically within 2×2\times), consistent with rank-invariance.
As with Init[A] and α=1\alpha=1, this small variation is attributable to the discrete learning rate grid.
Compared to the α=1\alpha=1 setting, the optimal learning rates under α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} are substantially larger.
We also observe that smaller ranks (e.g., r=4r=4) usually favor slightly smaller learning rates than larger ranks—opposite to the trend observed with α=1\alpha=1.
This likely reflects the finite-size effects: at smaller ranks, lower-order terms can exert a non-negligible influence on feature learning and suppress the optimal learning rate.
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3]
Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1 (Figures 5, 2(c))
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] In this case, the optimal learning rate should be independent of LoRA rank.
The empirical results confirm this prediction: across all models, the best learning rates for different ranks cluster tightly.
The small variation likely stems from learning rate grid resolution and finite-size effects.
Although both Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1 and Init[A] with α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} exhibit rank-invariant optimal learning rates, our theory shows they differ in width scaling: η∝n−1\eta\propto n^{-1} for the former versus η∝n−1/2\eta\propto n^{-1/2} for the latter.
For large nn, Init[B] thus requires substantially smaller learning rates, as our experiments confirm.
We also observe that Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1 is more tolerant of larger learning rates.
This stability is consistent with the theoretical finding that intermediate features remain order-one under Init[B], preventing internal activations from growing with width.
[id=S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1] Crucially, our theory reveals that FFT shares the same learning rate scaling η∝n−1\eta\propto n^{-1} with Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1, suggesting that their optimal learning rates may align and leading to learning rate transfer between the two.
Experiments support this conjecture: for most models, the optimal learning rates for Init[B] (α=1\alpha=1) align closely with those for FFT.
The exception is RoBERTa-large, where FFT favors a slightly smaller learning rate than Init[B].
We attribute this gap to the additional classification head: although its learning rate is fixed, jointly training it with LoRA adapters may still perturb the optimal learning rate.
Nevertheless, our experiments show that learning rates tuned for Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1 transfers effectively to FFT in most model architectures, with minimal performance degradation.

5.3 RLVR Results
[id=S5.SS3.p1.1] RLVR results are reported in Figure 6.
The learning rate sweeps reveal patterns consistent with our findings under SFT.
Under Init[A] with α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} (Figure 6(a)), the optimal learning rate is approximately rank-invariant: curves for different ranks peak at nearly the same learning rate.
Similarly, under Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1 (Figure 6(b)), the optimal learning rate is rank-invariant and aligns with the FFT optimum, suggesting that learning rates tuned with LoRA can transfer seamlessly to FFT.
For results of Init[A] with α=1\alpha=1, please kindly refer to Appendix D.1.
[id=S5.SS3.p2.1] Compared with SFT, RL finetuning is more sensitive to learning rate selection. In SFT, a learning rate that is too small simply slows convergence; in RLVR, however, overly large or small learning rates substantially degrade training reward.
Importantly, this sensitivity also manifests in training time.
As shown in Figure 6(c), the optimal learning rate incurs the shortest training time, while suboptimal rates can increase wall-clock time by 22–4×4\times.
The μ\muA scaling rules thus provide practical value beyond final performance: by identifying well-behaved learning rate regions in advance, practitioners can avoid time-consuming hyperparameter searches over suboptimal configurations.
We provide a detailed investigation on this phenomenon in Appendix D.2.
[id=S5.SS3.p3.1] Although LoRA and FFT have comparable per-step wall-clock times in our experiment, their memory footprints differ substantially.
Figure 6(d) shows that FFT consumes over 2×2\times the GPU memory of LoRA (r=256r{=}256), with most overhead attributable to gradient buffers and optimizer states.
This gap widens further at larger model sizes.
Our theory thus enables a practical workflow that exploits this difference: one can sweep learning rates using Init[B] with α=1\alpha{=}1 on mid-tier GPUs (e.g., A6000), which are more available and cost-effective, then transfer the optimal rate directly to FFT on higher-capacity hardware with minimal re-tuning.

6 Conclusion and Limitations
[id=S6.p1.1] This work proposes μ\muA (Maximal-Update Adaptation), a theoretical framework for LoRA finetuning that characterizes how the optimal learning rate scales with model width and adapter rank to achieve maximal feature updates.
Using this framework, we identify a LoRA configuration that enables learning rate transfer between LoRA and FFT.
Comprehensive experiments validate the μ\muA scaling rules and demonstrate effective learning rate transfer in practice.
[id=S6.p2.1] Our work has two main limitations. First, our theory is asymptotic and can be sensitive to noise for finite (n,r)(n,r).
Second, our analysis establishes a necessary condition for learning rate transfer; future work is needed to identify and prove sufficient conditions for a more complete theory.
Nevertheless, our experiments show strong agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical results.

[id=A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Purpose and scope.
[id=A1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] This appendix provides the detailed derivations supporting the theories in the main text.
We analyze the dynamics of LoRA finetuning in the limit where both the network width nn and the LoRA rank rr grow to infinity.
Our first goal is to ensure that the output features remain bounded throughout finetuning—that is, they do not explode as nn and rr increase.
Achieving this requires scaling the learning rate appropriately with nn and rr.
Our second goal is to ensure that the feature updates remain non-vanishing, so that learning proceeds efficiently and does not stall as the network grows.

[id=A2.SS2.p1.1] Throughout the paper, we analyze the LoRA-augmented weight matrix formulated as follows:
[id=A2.Ex174]
𝐖←𝐖+α​𝐁𝐀,\mathbf{W}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}+\alpha\,\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A},
[id=A2.SS2.p1.2] where 𝐀∈ℝr×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} and 𝐁∈ℝn×r\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} are rank-rr factors, and α\alpha is the LoRA multiplier.
[id=A2.SS2.p2.1] Our implementation uses the PEFT library (Mangrulkar et al., 2022), which internally parameterizes the update as
[id=A2.Ex175]
𝐖←𝐖+sr​𝐁𝐀,\mathbf{W}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}+\frac{s}{r}\,\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A},
[id=A2.SS2.p2.2] where ss corresponds to lora_alpha in LoraConfig. To achieve an effective multiplier α\alpha in our notation, we set s=α​rs=\alpha r. For example, constant multiplier α=1\alpha=1 requires lora_alpha=r{}=r, whereas rank-dependent multiplier α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1} requires lora_alpha=1{}=1.
In both cases, we set use_rslora=False.
[id=A2.SS2.p3.1] We study the three LoRA configurations described in Section 5.1:
[id=A2.I2.i1] •
[id=A2.I2.i1.p1.1] Init[A] with α=1\alpha=1: initialize 𝐀\mathbf{A} randomly and set 𝐁=𝟎\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}. Set lora_alpha to the rank used.
[id=A2.I2.i2] •
[id=A2.I2.i2.p1.1] Init[A] with α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1}: same initialization as above, but use a multiplier α=r−1\alpha=r^{-1}. Set lora_alpha to 1.
[id=A2.I2.i3] •
[id=A2.I2.i3.p1.1] Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1: initialize 𝐁\mathbf{B} randomly and set 𝐀=𝟎\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{0}. Set lora_alpha to the rank used.

B.4 Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RVLR) Setting
[id=A2.SS4.SSS0.Px1]
GSM8k (Llama-3.1-8B).
[id=A2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We finetune Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) with reinforcement learning using verifiable, rule-based rewards via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024).
Our experiments use the GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021) dataset, available as openai/gsm8k1414
14
https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k.
This dataset contains 8.58.5k grade-school math problems paired with their solutions.
We randomly sample the 500500 training problems and 5050 test problems for our training and validation splits, respectively.
Each problem is converted into a prompt using a template we design to elicit the model’s reasoning; the prompt template is summarized in Table 5.
We compute a scalar reward for each sampled completion and sum over two rule-based components:
[id=A2.I4.i1] •
[id=A2.I4.i1.p1.1] Accuracy reward: assigns +1+1 when the extracted final answer matches the reference, and 00 otherwise.
[id=A2.I4.i2] •
[id=A2.I4.i2.p1.1] Format reward: assigns +0.1+0.1 when the completion places reasoning within <think>...</think> tags and the final answer within <answer>...</answer> tags, and 00 otherwise.
[id=A2.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] For each prompt, we sample 88 completions from the current policy using temperature 1.01.0, with no nucleus truncation (top-p=1.0p=1.0), no top-kk truncation (top-k=0k=0), and repetition penalty 1.01.0.
We set the maximum completion length to 10241024 tokens and standardize rewards within each prompt’s sample group.
We use the DAPO variant (Yu et al., 2025) of the GRPO loss, which uses a token-level loss to accommodate longer sequences.
We set weight decay to 00, as it strongly degraded performance in our experiments.
We omit the KL penalty term since it provides minimal benefit while increasing memory overhead by requiring a reference model to be loaded.

15
https://huggingface.co/datasets/lambdalabs/naruto-blip-captions.
The dataset contains 1.21.2k image–caption pairs; we reserve 8%8\% for validation.
Images are resized and cropped to 512×512512\times 512, then encoded into the latent space of the pretrained VAE (Kingma and Welling, 2014).

[id=A2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We sweep the learning rate on a l​o​g2log_{2} grid (i.e., adjacent points differ by a factor of two).
The grid range varies across LoRA configurations, models, and tasks, chosen to span from peak training performance to the onset of divergence.

For language modeling tasks, we report final training loss (EMA-smoothed with a smoothing factor of 0.10.1) and validation NLL. For classification, we report final training loss (EMA-smoothed) and validation accuracy.
For diffusion, we report validation FID.
For RLVR tasks, we report final training reward (EMA-smoothed) and test reward.
We select the optimal learning rate separately for each metric.

[id=A2.SS6.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] To manage computational cost, we evaluate each configuration over a small grid of LoRA ranks, using 5 ranks in total.

D.2 Case Study on the Relationship between Learning Rate and Training Time
[id=A4.SS2.p1.1] In our experiment, we found that a suboptimal learning rate usually causes a longer training time under RLVR.
We attribute this to a two-phase training pattern we find: in the first phase, the model explores the solution space by generating long sequences (often hitting the maximum generation limit); in the second phase, once the model learns to solve the task, it produces more concise solutions that are 44–5×5\times shorter.
At near-optimal learning rates, the model quickly exits the exploratory phase, whereas at suboptimal rates it remains stuck and continues generating long sequences, prolonging each training step.
Here, we conduct a case study examining this phenomenon. We compare FFT and Init[B] (with constant α=1\alpha=1 and rank r=256r=256) under two learning rate settings: the optimal rate (η=2−18\eta=2^{-18}) and a suboptimal rate (η=2−16\eta=2^{-16}).
[id=A4.SS2.p2.1] As shown in Figures 15(a) and 15(b), training and test rewards collapse to near zero under the suboptimal learning rate, whereas they steadily increase under the optimal rate. More importantly, with the optimal learning rate, the training exhibits the two-phase pattern discussed above: as shown in Figure 15(c), completion lengths initially approach the maximum generation limit (10241024 tokens) during early exploration (steps <50<50), then sharply decrease to approximately 200 tokens (a 44–5×5\times reduction) around step 100 as the model learns to produce concise solutions. In contrast, models trained with the suboptimal learning rate remain stuck in the exploratory phase, consistently generating maximum-length completions throughout training. This directly translates to longer per-step training times, as shown in Figure 15(d): models with optimal learning rates require only 4–5 seconds per step, while those with suboptimal rates require 15–22 seconds—a 33–5×5\times increase.
[id=A4.SS2.p3.1] In Table 8, we sample responses from the model to a fixed question during full finetuning with optimal and suboptimal learning rates.
With the optimal learning rate, the model first learns to follow the specified format, then attempts to solve the problem, and finally learns to simplify its solution.
In contrast, with the suboptimal learning rate, the model fails to follow the specified response format at the beginning and eventually collapses into repetitive token generation.
[id=A4.SS2.p4.1] We note one exception: Init[B] with α=1\alpha=1 and a higher learning rate (η=2−15\eta=2^{-15}) also exhibits shorter per-step training times.
However, this represents the opposite failure mode—rather than remaining stuck at maximum-length generations, the model collapses and stops generation almost immediately, producing completions of ∼\sim2 tokens, as shown in Figure 16.
